claims.text: Chromium and aluminum are candidate protective oxide-forming elements in high-entropy alloys.
Selective oxidation of specific oxide-forming elements governs protective oxide-scale formation.
Selective oxidation of specific oxide-forming elements governs protective oxide-scale stability.
The proposed selective-oxidation behavior enhances surface diffusion.
Favorable redox kinetics contribute to formation and stability of the protective oxide scale.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements in their metallic state.
Systematically changing the concentration of a candidate oxide former in otherwise similar HEAs provides a controlled comparison.
Oxide composition, thickness, continuity, and adherence mediate oxidation resistance.
Higher concentrations of candidate oxide-forming elements increase surface diffusion.
Higher concentrations of candidate oxide-forming elements promote rapid oxidation that forms a coherent, adherent, and continuous oxide scale.
A coherent, adherent, and continuous oxide scale acts as a barrier against further oxidation.
Lower concentrations of candidate oxide-forming elements produce discontinuous or less-protective oxide scales.
Increasing candidate oxide-former content will produce a thicker oxide scale than the baseline.
Increasing candidate oxide-former content will produce a more continuous and better-adherent oxide scale than the baseline.
Increasing candidate oxide-former content will reduce oxidation weight gain relative to lower-content HEAs or conventional-alloy baselines.
The proposed mechanism applies under oxygen-rich conditions between approximately 800°C and 1100°C.
The proposed mechanism applies only within a compositional domain in which HEA multicomponent effects are maintained.
Failure of increased oxide-former content to significantly improve scale integrity and reduce oxidation weight gain relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
